title: United States | Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and AML Compliance
tagline: Know the US rulebook: BSA program pillars, CIP and beneficial ownership, EDD, SARs, CTRs, records and OFAC sanctions for bank staff.
description:
This quest teaches the **US Bank Secrecy Act (BSA)** framework as it applies to banks, built on the FinCEN rules in 31 CFR Chapter X, the Federal Reserve's BSA program rule (12 CFR 208.63) and the parallel OCC and FDIC rules, OFAC's sanctions guidance and the FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual that examiners work from.

You will work through the five pillars of a bank's BSA/AML program, the Customer Identification Program, customer due diligence and beneficial ownership, special due diligence for foreign correspondent and private banking accounts, the shell bank ban, suspicious activity reports and their confidentiality, currency transaction reports, BSA records, OFAC blocking and reporting, and the April 2026 **proposed** AML/CFT program rule (not final at the time of review).

It is meant for staff of US banks whose work the BSA touches: branch, onboarding, operations, payments, correspondent and private banking, BSA/AML and sanctions teams, and managers who oversee them. The BSA program rules require training for appropriate personnel, and examiners check it. This quest builds knowledge and does not replace your bank's own BSA/AML and sanctions policies and procedures.
audience: Branch, account opening and digital onboarding staff at US banks
Wire room, payments and cash operations staff
Correspondent banking and private banking relationship teams
BSA/AML analysts, investigators and sanctions screening staff
Managers, BSA officers and board members who oversee the BSA/AML program
outcomes: Explain who writes, examines and enforces US BSA/AML and sanctions rules and name the five pillars of a bank's program
Apply CIP, CDD and beneficial ownership rules correctly when opening accounts for individuals and legal entities
Decide when correspondent and private banking accounts need enhanced due diligence and recognise the shell bank ban
Escalate unusual activity, apply SAR and CTR thresholds and deadlines, and protect SAR confidentiality
Handle an OFAC match from block or reject to report, and support testing, training and exam readiness
Describe what the April 2026 proposed AML/CFT program rule would change, and that it is not yet final

quest.name: The Examiner's Visit
quest.premise: You have just joined the BSA/AML team of Bramblecove Bank, N.A., a fictional national bank headquartered in Columbus, Ohio, with branches in Chicago, Houston and Miami and a correspondent and private banking desk in Miami. The OCC has announced its BSA/AML examination. BSA Officer Dana Whitfield wants you ready: with investigator Marcus Bell, branch manager Elena Ruiz, correspondent banking head Kevin Nguyen and sanctions manager Amina Yusuf, clear five stages and then face the final boss: the examiner's questions.

badge.name: BSA Gatekeeper
badge.description: Awarded to US bank staff who can apply the BSA program, CIP and CDD, EDD, SAR, CTR, records and OFAC rules with confidence.

cast.name: Kevin Nguyen
cast.role: Head of Correspondent and Private Banking

sessions.title: The BSA Framework, Regulators and the Program Pillars
sessions.summary: Who writes, examines and enforces US BSA/AML rules, and the five pillars every bank's board-approved BSA/AML program must contain.
objectives: Explain the roles of FinCEN, the OCC, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, OFAC and the FFIEC manual
List the minimum elements of a bank's BSA/AML program under 31 CFR 1020.210 and the agency rules
Describe the board's role in approving and resourcing the program
Recognise why monitoring must follow risk rather than staffing

cards.title: Day one: the letter from the OCC
cards.setting: BSA/AML department, Bramblecove Bank head office, Columbus, Ohio. 8:45 am.

lines.text: Your access badge works on the second try. On your desk: a laptop, a binder labelled BSA PROGRAM, and a printed letter.
Welcome. I'm Dana Whitfield, the bank's BSA Officer. That letter is from the OCC. They are coming to examine our BSA/AML program.
Marcus Bell, investigations. Before you ask: yes, the OCC examines us, but FinCEN writes most of the rules we follow. It confuses everyone at first.
Kevin Nguyen, correspondent and private banking. My only question is whether this exam slows down my foreign bank onboarding.
It will if our program has gaps. Examiners don't just read our policy. They test whether each pillar actually works.
Stage one is the Charter Room: who makes the rules, who checks them, and the five pillars every bank program needs. Ready?

cards.title: The US BSA system in five scenes

scenes.heading: The law
scenes.narration: The Bank Secrecy Act is the main US anti-money laundering law. Congress wrote it and later strengthened it, for example through the USA PATRIOT Act. It tells banks to keep records, file reports and run an anti-money laundering program.

scenes.heading: FinCEN writes the rules
scenes.narration: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, a bureau of the Treasury, administers the BSA. Its rules for banks sit in Title 31 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Chapter X, mostly in Parts 1010 and 1020.

scenes.heading: Your supervisor examines
scenes.narration: Your bank's federal supervisor examines BSA compliance under authority delegated by FinCEN and under its own banking law powers. National banks have the OCC, state member banks the Federal Reserve, and state non-member banks the FDIC.

scenes.heading: The FFIEC manual guides examiners
scenes.narration: The FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual tells examiners how to assess a program. It is guidance for examiners, not a regulation, but it shows you what they will look for.

scenes.heading: OFAC runs sanctions
scenes.narration: Sanctions are a separate Treasury office, OFAC. Its rules apply to all US persons, banks included, and its penalties can apply even when nobody knew they were breaking a sanction.

cards.title: Who does what in US BSA/AML
headers: Role for a bank like Bramblecove

items.label: FinCEN
items.left: FinCEN (Treasury)
items.right: Administers the BSA, writes 31 CFR Chapter X rules, receives SARs and CTRs, enforces civil penalties

items.label: OCC
items.left: OCC
items.right: Supervises national banks such as Bramblecove; examines BSA compliance and has its own BSA program rule

items.label: Federal Reserve
items.left: Federal Reserve
items.right: Supervises state member banks and holding companies; BSA program rule in 12 CFR 208.63

items.label: FDIC
items.left: FDIC
items.right: Supervises state non-member banks; BSA program rule in 12 CFR 326.8

items.label: OFAC
items.left: OFAC (Treasury)
items.right: Administers and enforces sanctions; publishes the SDN List; receives blocked and rejected transaction reports

items.label: FFIEC
items.left: FFIEC
items.right: Publishes the interagency BSA/AML Examination Manual that examiners use

cards.question: Bramblecove Bank is a national bank. Which agency will lead its BSA/AML examination?
options: The FDIC, because it insures the bank's deposits
The OCC, because it supervises national banks
FinCEN, because it writes the BSA rules
OFAC, because the exam covers sanctions
cards.explanation: The OCC supervises national banks and examines their BSA compliance under authority delegated by FinCEN and its own powers. FinCEN writes the rules and can enforce them, but day-to-day examination of a national bank is the OCC's job.

cards.title: The program rule: five pillars and a board signature
cards.body:
FinCEN's rule for banks, **31 CFR 1020.210**, says a bank with a federal regulator meets the BSA program duty if its program includes, at a minimum:

- a **system of internal controls** to assure ongoing compliance
- **independent testing**, by bank personnel or an outside party
- a **designated individual** (the BSA officer) coordinating and monitoring day-to-day compliance
- **training for appropriate personnel**
- **risk-based ongoing customer due diligence**

The bank must also comply with its own supervisor's program rule. The Federal Reserve's rule, **12 CFR 208.63**, requires a **written** program, **approved by the board** and **noted in the minutes**, with the same four core elements. The OCC (12 CFR 21.21) and the FDIC (12 CFR 326.8) have their own rules for the banks they supervise.

The CIP and the special due diligence rules for correspondent and private banking accounts all sit inside this program.

cards.title: Building a BSA/AML program
cards.caption: The board-approved written program sits on top; each pillar below must work in practice.

items.label: Written, board-approved program
items.detail: Approved by the board and noted in the minutes (Fed rule 12 CFR 208.63(b)(1))

items.label: Internal controls
items.detail: Policies, procedures and systems such as CIP, monitoring, reporting and records

items.label: Independent testing
items.detail: Tests the program; done by bank staff independent of the function or by an outside party

items.label: BSA officer
items.detail: Named person coordinating and monitoring day-to-day compliance

items.label: Training
items.detail: For appropriate personnel, matched to their roles

items.label: Ongoing CDD
items.detail: Customer risk profiles, ongoing monitoring and updating customer information on a risk basis

cards.title: Match the pillar to the evidence
cards.prompt: An examiner asks for evidence of each pillar. Match each pillar to the document that best proves it works.

pairs.right: Alert-handling procedures and system rules, with logs showing alerts were worked on time
A report by an auditor outside the BSA function, with findings and management responses
A board resolution naming the BSA officer, plus reports showing their authority and resources
Role-based materials, attendance records and assessment results for staff and directors
Customer risk profiles that were updated when activity or ownership changed

cards.title: Kevin's shortcut
cards.setting: Leadership huddle, 4th floor, Columbus. The alert queue screen shows 3,400 open alerts.

lines.text: Our monitoring system is flooding the team. Why not cap it at 200 alerts a day? Whatever is in the queue after that can wait.
Because the riskiest customer might be alert 201. A cap decides what we look at based on staffing, not risk.
Then we tune the system so it generates fewer alerts. Same thing, right?
Not the same. Tuning based on tested risk analysis, documented and approved, is fine. A cap set by headcount is not. And hiring is a board-level resourcing question.
Let's think it through properly. What would you do?

cards.title: The alert cap
cards.situation: Bramblecove's transaction monitoring backlog has grown to 3,400 alerts. Kevin proposes a daily cap of 200 alerts, with excess alerts suppressed until volumes fall. Two analysts have resigned. The OCC exam starts in six weeks. You are asked for your recommendation.

choices.text: Support the cap for now; the backlog will look smaller before the exam
choices.outcome: Capping alerts by headcount means high-risk activity may never be reviewed and suspicious activity goes unreported. Regulators have penalised banks for exactly this. It also hides the problem from the board.

choices.text: Reject the cap, report the backlog and staffing gap to senior management and the board, and request resources and a documented, risk-based tuning review
choices.outcome: Best answer. The board approves the program and must know it lacks resources. Tuning based on documented risk analysis is legitimate; suppressing alerts to match staffing is not.

choices.text: Ask analysts to close older alerts quickly without full review so the queue clears
choices.outcome: This trades one failure for another: poorly reviewed alerts can mean missed SARs, and examiners test alert decisions, not only queue sizes.

choices.text: Reject the cap and ask the team to work overtime until the exam, without escalating
choices.outcome: Partly right: you avoided the cap. But overtime is not a sustainable control, and the board and senior management need to know about a resourcing gap in a required program.

cards.title: Real case: U.S. Bank's alert caps and a personal penalty
cards.body:
In **2020 FinCEN** assessed a civil money penalty of **USD 450,000** against **Michael LaFontaine**, a former Chief Compliance Officer and later Chief Operational Risk Officer at U.S. Bank National Association.

FinCEN found that the bank had **capped the number of alerts** its automated transaction monitoring system produced, so some high-risk customers did not generate alerts simply because others scored even higher. The caps let the bank hire fewer investigators. The OCC had repeatedly warned bank officials against numerical caps. FinCEN also found the BSA compliance function was not adequately staffed, and that he shared responsibility for the bank's failures to maintain an effective program and file SARs on time.

**Lessons for you:**
- monitoring must follow risk, not available headcount
- people in charge of a BSA program can be held personally responsible
- resourcing gaps belong in front of senior management and the board

Source: FinCEN enforcement action 2020-01 (fincen.gov).

cards.title: How a BSA rule reaches your desk

items.label: Statute
items.detail: Congress passes the BSA and later amendments

items.label: FinCEN rule
items.detail: Treasury's FinCEN writes the detailed rules in 31 CFR Chapter X

items.label: Agency rule
items.detail: OCC, Fed and FDIC program rules apply to the banks each supervises

items.label: Exam guidance
items.detail: The FFIEC manual shows examiners how to test the program

items.label: Bank policy
items.detail: Your board-approved BSA/AML program turns rules into bank policy

items.label: Your procedure
items.detail: Desk procedures tell you exactly what to do in your role

cards.front: Myth: the FFIEC manual is a regulation.
cards.back: Fact: it is interagency guidance for examiners. The binding duties come from the BSA and the FinCEN and agency rules, but the manual shows how examiners judge compliance.

cards.front: Myth: OFAC is part of FinCEN.
cards.back: Fact: both are in the Treasury, but OFAC is a separate office that administers and enforces sanctions programs.

cards.front: Myth: training is nice to have.
cards.back: Fact: training for appropriate personnel is a required element of every bank's BSA program.

cards.front: Myth: the board only needs a yearly summary.
cards.back: Fact: the board approves the written program (noted in the minutes under the Fed rule) and should get enough information to oversee it.

cards.front: Myth: independent testing must be done by an outside firm.
cards.back: Fact: the rules allow testing by bank personnel or an outside party; what matters is that testers are independent of the BSA function.

cards.front: Myth: CFT is a separate program.
cards.back: Fact: countering terrorist financing runs through the same BSA program, for example the CIP check against government terrorist lists.

cards.question: Which of these is NOT one of the minimum program elements listed in the Federal Reserve's BSA program rule?
options: Independent testing by bank personnel or an outside party
A designated person responsible for day-to-day compliance
An annual BSA audit by an external accounting firm
Training for appropriate personnel
cards.explanation: The rule requires independent testing but lets the bank use its own personnel or an outside party. It does not require an external accounting firm or set an annual frequency. The other three are listed elements.

cards.title: Keep your own rule map
cards.body:
Rules move. In 2025 and 2026 alone FinCEN issued SAR FAQs, relief on beneficial ownership and a proposed program rule.

- Read rules in **official copies**: FinCEN's site and the Federal Reserve Regulatory Service publish the 31 CFR text.
- Note **which rule** your procedure comes from, so you can check it when it changes.
- Treat proposals as proposals until a **final rule** is published.

cards.title: Charter Room cleared
items: FinCEN administers the BSA and writes the bank rules in 31 CFR Chapter X; your federal supervisor examines you.
National banks: OCC. State member banks: Federal Reserve. State non-member banks: FDIC. Sanctions: OFAC.
Five pillars: internal controls, independent testing, a BSA officer, training and risk-based ongoing CDD.
The program is written and board-approved; resourcing gaps must reach senior management and the board.
Alert caps set by staffing, not risk, have led to penalties for banks and for individuals.

cards.prompt: Think about your own role. Which BSA pillar does your daily work feed into most, and what evidence of your work would an examiner ask to see?

quiz.question: Which US body administers the Bank Secrecy Act and writes the bank rules in 31 CFR Chapter X?
options: The OCC, as the national bank supervisor
FinCEN, a bureau of the Treasury
OFAC, as the Treasury sanctions office
The FFIEC, through its examination manual
quiz.explanation: FinCEN administers the BSA and issues its implementing rules in 31 CFR Chapter X. The OCC examines national banks, OFAC handles sanctions, and the FFIEC manual is examiner guidance.

quiz.question: A state-chartered bank is a member of the Federal Reserve System. Which program rule sets its BSA compliance program requirements alongside FinCEN's rule?
options: 12 CFR 326.8, the FDIC's rule
12 CFR 21.21, the OCC's rule
31 CFR 501.603, the OFAC rule
12 CFR 208.63, the Federal Reserve's rule
quiz.explanation: State member banks are supervised by the Federal Reserve, whose BSA program rule is 12 CFR 208.63. The FDIC rule covers state non-member banks, the OCC rule national banks, and 31 CFR 501.603 is an OFAC reporting rule.

quiz.question: Under the Federal Reserve's rule, what must happen to a state member bank's BSA compliance program?
options: It must be in writing, approved by the board of directors and noted in the minutes
It must be approved by FinCEN before use
It must be filed with the FFIEC each year and countersigned by the bank's external auditor before use
It must be signed by the external auditor
quiz.explanation: 12 CFR 208.63(b)(1) requires a written program approved by the board and noted in the minutes. There is no FinCEN pre-approval or annual filing with the FFIEC.

quiz.question: Which list contains only elements that 31 CFR 1020.210 requires in a bank's AML program?
options: Internal controls, a compliance committee, an annual external audit, training for all staff and a whistleblower hotline
Independent testing, a sanctions officer, quarterly board reports and customer exit procedures
Internal controls, independent testing, a designated compliance individual, training and risk-based ongoing CDD
Training, transaction monitoring software, a fraud team and an ethics code
quiz.explanation: The rule lists internal controls, independent testing, designation of a person for day-to-day compliance, training for appropriate personnel and risk-based ongoing CDD. The other lists add items the rule does not name.

quiz.question: Bramblecove's head of audit proposes that a senior analyst from the BSA team test the BSA program this year to save money. What is the main problem?
options: The rule requires that independent testing be performed by an outside accounting firm, not bank staff
Testing may only be done by the OCC
The tester would not be independent of the function being tested
Analysts may not see audit reports
quiz.explanation: The rules let testing be done by bank personnel or an outside party, so internal staff are acceptable, but the people testing must be independent of the BSA function. An analyst testing their own team's work is not independent.

quiz.question: A board member says, 'The FFIEC manual is just a book; we only need to follow FinCEN.' What is the best reply?
options: The manual is examiner guidance, not a rule, but it shows how examiners will judge whether the program meets the rules
The manual is a binding regulation issued by FinCEN
The manual is a binding interagency regulation, so any difference from it is a violation of law in itself, whatever the rules say
The manual applies only to the Federal Reserve's banks
quiz.explanation: The FFIEC BSA/AML Examination Manual is interagency guidance for examiners. It does not create new legal duties, but it tells banks what examiners expect to see.

quiz.question: Bramblecove's monitoring team wants to cap alerts at the number analysts can clear each day. Why do examiners and FinCEN treat this as a failure?
options: Caps are only allowed for banks below a set asset size
Caps are acceptable as long as the board approves them and the cap level is written into the minutes each year
Caps breach OFAC rules rather than BSA rules
It lets staffing, not risk, decide which activity is reviewed, so suspicious activity can go unreported
quiz.explanation: In the U.S. Bank matter, FinCEN found that alert caps tied to staffing meant high-risk customers might never alert. Monitoring must follow risk; resourcing gaps must be fixed, not hidden.

quiz.question: In the 2020 FinCEN action against Michael LaFontaine, what was notable?
options: The bank's charter was revoked
A civil money penalty was imposed on an individual former compliance and risk officer
OFAC imposed the penalty for sanctions breaches
The case concerned a credit union that failed to verify identities under its Customer Identification Program
quiz.explanation: FinCEN assessed USD 450,000 against a former Chief Compliance Officer and Chief Operational Risk Officer of U.S. Bank, showing that individuals can be held responsible for BSA program failures.

quiz.question: A new employee asks why counter-terrorist financing is part of Bramblecove's BSA program rather than a separate program. Which answer is accurate?
options: The same BSA program, including the CIP check against government terrorist lists, covers both AML and CFT
CFT is handled only by OFAC, so the BSA program ignores it
CFT applies only to banks with foreign branches
The BSA program will only cover terrorist financing once the April 2026 proposal to rename it an AML/CFT program becomes final
quiz.explanation: Terrorist financing is in scope of the existing BSA program; for example, the CIP must check customers against federal lists of known or suspected terrorists. The 2026 proposal would rename the program but does not create CFT duties from scratch.

quiz.question: The BSA officer reports that the team cannot keep up with alerts. Senior management decides not to tell the board until after the OCC exam. What is the main weakness?
options: Nothing is wrong, since staffing and resourcing are management matters that the board does not need to hear about
The OCC must be told first, before the board
The board, which approves the program, is denied information it needs to oversee and resource it
The BSA officer should have capped the alerts instead
quiz.explanation: The board approves the BSA program and is expected to oversee and resource it. Hiding a resourcing gap undermines oversight and is a pattern seen in enforcement actions such as U.S. Bank and Shinhan.

sessions.title: CIP, Customer Due Diligence and Beneficial Ownership
sessions.summary: Identify and verify customers under the CIP, identify the beneficial owners of legal entity customers, and keep customer risk profiles current.
objectives: Apply the CIP's minimum information, verification, list-check, notice and record rules
Identify beneficial owners under the 25% ownership and control prongs
Know when the bank may rely on a customer's certification and when it may not
Explain ongoing CDD and the 2026 changes to beneficial ownership

cards.title: Two customers at the Miami branch
cards.setting: Bramblecove Bank, Brickell branch, Miami. 10:20 am.

lines.text: (video call) Dana, two tricky ones. A man wants a checking account but has no photo ID with him, only a utility bill and a bank card.
And Brightwater Logistics LLC wants a business account. The signer says the owners are 'a group of investors' and he'd rather not list them.
Two different rules. The first is the Customer Identification Program. The second adds the beneficial ownership rule for legal entity customers.
And after both are open, customer due diligence keeps going: what is the account for, and does the activity match?
Stage two is the Front Door. Get this right and half of every later investigation gets easier.

scenes.heading: Collect before opening
scenes.narration: Before opening an account, the bank collects at least four items: name, date of birth for an individual, an address, and an identification number. For a US person that number is a taxpayer identification number.

scenes.heading: Verify within a reasonable time
scenes.narration: The bank then verifies identity within a reasonable time after opening, using documents, non-documentary methods or both, so it can form a reasonable belief that it knows who the customer really is.

scenes.heading: When verification fails
scenes.narration: The CIP must say when not to open an account, what the customer may do while verification is pending, when to close the account, and when to file a SAR.

scenes.heading: Check government lists
scenes.narration: The CIP must check whether the customer appears on any federal list of known or suspected terrorists designated by Treasury, and follow any directives that come with those lists.

scenes.heading: Notice and records
scenes.narration: Customers get adequate notice that the bank asks for identifying information, before the account is opened. The bank records what it collected, how it verified, and how it resolved any discrepancy.

items.label: Collect identifying information
items.detail: Name, date of birth (individuals), address, identification number, before opening

items.label: Verify identity
items.detail: Documents, non-documentary methods or both, within a reasonable time after opening

items.label: Handle failed verification
items.detail: When not to open, terms while pending, when to close, when to file a SAR

items.label: Compare with government lists
items.detail: Federal lists of known or suspected terrorists designated by Treasury

items.label: Give customer notice
items.detail: Adequate notice before the account is opened, e.g. lobby, website or application

items.label: Keep records
items.detail: Identifying data, documents relied on, methods and results, discrepancy resolution

cards.question: A non-US individual opens an account at Bramblecove. Which identification number may the CIP accept?
options: Only a US taxpayer identification number
A taxpayer identification number, a passport number with country of issuance, an alien identification card number, or another qualifying government ID number
Any number the customer provides, verified later
No number is needed if the customer shows a photo ID
cards.explanation: For a non-US person the CIP rule lists several acceptable numbers: a taxpayer identification number, a passport number and issuing country, an alien identification card number, or the number and issuing country of another government document with a photograph or similar safeguard.

cards.title: Documentary or non-documentary?
cards.prompt: Sort each verification method into the type the CIP rule describes.

items.text: Unexpired passport
Unexpired driver's license
Certified articles of incorporation for a company
Government-issued business license
Comparing the customer's data with a consumer reporting agency
Checking references with another financial institution
Contacting the customer
Obtaining a financial statement

cards.title: Beneficial ownership: who really owns and controls
cards.body:
Under **31 CFR 1010.230**, banks must identify and verify the **beneficial owners** of each **legal entity customer** when a new account is opened. A beneficial owner is:

- **Ownership prong:** each individual who directly or indirectly owns **25% or more** of the equity interests (there may be none)
- **Control prong:** **one** individual with significant responsibility to control, manage or direct the entity, such as a CEO, CFO, managing member or president

If a **trust** owns 25% or more, the **trustee** is treated as the owner. Some customers are excluded (for example regulated financial institutions and SEC-registered issuers), and certain entities such as nonprofits are subject only to the control prong.

The person opening the account certifies the information. The bank verifies each beneficial owner's identity with risk-based procedures that include the CIP elements, and may use photocopies of documents. It may **rely** on the customer's information unless it knows of facts that reasonably call it into question.

items.label: Who
items.left: Every customer opening an account
items.right: Individuals behind each legal entity customer

items.label: What
items.left: Name, date of birth, address, ID number
items.right: Each 25%+ owner and one control person

items.label: How
items.left: Documents and/or non-documentary methods
items.right: Certification by the opener, then risk-based verification

items.label: Records
items.left: Identifying data kept 5 years after account closes
items.right: Identification records kept 5 years after account closes

items.label: Verification records
items.left: Kept 5 years after the record is made
items.right: Kept 5 years after the record is made

cards.title: Opening Brightwater Logistics LLC
cards.prompt: Put the beneficial ownership steps for a new legal entity account in a sensible order.
steps: Confirm Brightwater is a legal entity customer and not an excluded type
Run CIP on the entity itself: name, address, identification number and entity documents
Obtain the certification of each 25%+ owner and one control person from the person opening the account
Verify each beneficial owner's identity using the bank's risk-based CIP procedures
Resolve discrepancies or escalate if facts call the certification into question
Record the certification, verification methods and results, and build the customer risk profile

cards.title: Who owns Brightwater?
cards.setting: Brickell branch, Miami. The next morning.

lines.text: The signer came back. He certified: Rosa Delgado 30%, two brothers with 24% each, and a family trust with 22%. CEO is Paul Marsh.
So the ownership prong gives us one name, and the control prong one more. The trust is under 25%, so no trustee needed for this rule.
Here's the snag. Our onboarding analyst found a local news story saying the brothers sold their stakes last month to a Panama company.
Then we know of facts that call the certification into question. Reliance is gone for now. What do we do?

cards.question: Brightwater is owned 30% by Rosa, 24% each by two brothers and 22% by a family trust; Paul Marsh is CEO. Under the CDD rule, whom must the bank identify as beneficial owners?
options: All four owners and Paul Marsh
Rosa (ownership prong) and Paul Marsh (control prong)
Rosa only, because she is the only owner above 25%
Paul Marsh only, because the control person replaces the owners
cards.explanation: Only individuals owning 25% or more meet the ownership prong, so Rosa qualifies and the brothers do not. A single control person, here the CEO, must also be identified. The trust is under 25%, so its trustee is not a beneficial owner under the ownership prong.

cards.title: The certification that no longer fits
cards.situation: Brightwater's signer certified its owners, but a news report says two owners recently sold their stakes to a Panama company. The signer says the paperwork 'is still being finalised' and asks Elena to open the account today with the original certification.

choices.text: Open the account today; the certification is signed and the bank may rely on it
choices.outcome: Reliance only holds when the bank has no knowledge of facts reasonably calling the information into question. The news report is such a fact, so relying on it now is a mistake.

choices.text: Ask for an updated certification covering the new Panama company's owners, verify them, and escalate to BSA/AML if the customer refuses or the picture stays unclear
choices.outcome: Best answer. The bank must identify the individuals who now own 25% or more, even through a foreign company, and follow its CIP and escalation procedures if it cannot.

choices.text: Open the account but flag it for review in a year
choices.outcome: Partly better than ignoring it, but the beneficial ownership duty applies at account opening, and a year is too late to resolve a known discrepancy.

choices.text: Refuse the account and tell the signer you suspect money laundering
choices.outcome: Refusing may become right if the customer will not cooperate, but telling him you suspect laundering could tip him off and is not how the bank handles a discrepancy.

cards.title: Ongoing CDD and what changed in 2026
cards.body:
The program rule requires **risk-based ongoing CDD**: understand the **nature and purpose** of each relationship to build a **customer risk profile**, and **monitor** on an ongoing basis to identify and report suspicious transactions and, on a risk basis, **update customer information**, including beneficial owners.

Two recent changes matter at the front door:

- **February 2026 exceptive relief:** FinCEN said banks generally need not re-identify and re-verify the beneficial owners of an **existing** legal entity customer each time it opens a **new account**, unless risk calls for it.
- **Corporate Transparency Act:** FinCEN's 2026 final rule made permanent the exemption of US companies and US persons from BOI reporting, so only foreign reporting companies file. This does **not** remove the bank's own duty under 31 CFR 1010.230.

cards.title: Front door vocabulary
cards.prompt: Match each term to its meaning in US BSA rules.

pairs.right: A corporation, LLC or other entity created by a filing with a Secretary of State or similar office, a general partnership, or a similar foreign entity
One individual with significant responsibility to control, manage or direct the entity
The bank's understanding of the nature and purpose of the relationship, used to judge whether activity is unusual
Relying on another regulated institution's CIP, when reasonable and backed by a contract with annual certification
Telling customers, before opening, that the bank asks for information to verify identity

cards.title: Numbers that matter at the front door

items.label: CIP data items
items.detail: Name, date of birth (individuals), address and identification number, before opening

items.label: Ownership prong
items.detail: Each individual owning 25% or more of the equity interests

items.label: Control prong
items.detail: A single individual who controls, manages or directs the entity

items.label: Identifying records
items.detail: Kept for five years after the account is closed

items.label: Verification records
items.detail: Kept for five years after the record is made

cards.front: The man has no photo ID with him. Must Elena refuse?
cards.back: Not automatically. The CIP must have non-documentary procedures for customers without unexpired photo ID; she follows them or the failed-verification steps.

cards.front: A US company is exempt from filing BOI with FinCEN. Is it exempt from the bank's beneficial ownership check?
cards.back: No. The bank's duty under 31 CFR 1010.230 is separate and continues.

cards.front: Does every legal entity have a 25% owner?
cards.back: No. There may be no individual at 25% or more, but the bank must still identify one control person.

cards.front: Can the bank verify a beneficial owner from a photocopy of a driver's license?
cards.back: Yes. For beneficial owners, documentary verification may use photocopies or other reproductions.

cards.front: When must the terrorist list check happen?
cards.back: Within a reasonable period after opening, or earlier if another federal law, regulation or directive requires it.

cards.title: Front Door unlocked
items: CIP: collect four core items before opening, verify within a reasonable time, check government lists, give notice and keep records.
Beneficial owners: every 25%+ owner plus one control person for each legal entity customer at account opening.
You may rely on the certification unless you know facts that reasonably call it into question.
Ongoing CDD means a risk profile, ongoing monitoring and risk-based updates, including beneficial owners.
CTA BOI filing now covers only foreign reporting companies; the bank's own beneficial ownership duty remains.

cards.prompt: Recall a customer or account you handled where the paperwork was complete but something did not fit. What fact would have taken away your right to rely on what the customer told you?

quiz.question: Which four items must Bramblecove obtain, at a minimum, from an individual US customer before opening an account under the CIP rule?
options: Name, address, phone number and employer
Name, passport number, email and source of funds
Name, date of birth, occupation and expected activity
Name, date of birth, address and taxpayer identification number
quiz.explanation: The CIP rule requires name, date of birth for individuals, an address and an identification number, which for a US person is a taxpayer identification number.

quiz.question: When must the bank verify a new customer's identity under the CIP rule?
options: Within a reasonable time after the account is opened
Before collecting any identifying information
Only if the account becomes suspicious
Within one year of opening
quiz.explanation: The CIP requires procedures to verify identity within a reasonable time after opening. The identifying information itself is collected before opening.

quiz.question: A customer opens an account online and cannot present any photo ID in person. What must the CIP provide for?
options: Automatic refusal of all remote applicants
Acceptance of the customer's own statement of identity until the account produces activity serious enough for a SAR
Non-documentary verification procedures for situations such as accounts opened without appearing in person
Verification only by a notary
quiz.explanation: The rule says non-documentary procedures must address customers who cannot present unexpired photo ID, accounts opened without documents, and customers who do not appear in person.

quiz.question: An LLC customer certifies three owners at 40%, 35% and 25%, and a managing member who controls the business. How many beneficial owners must the bank identify, assuming the managing member owns nothing?
options: Two: the largest owner and the managing member
Four: the three owners and the managing member
Three: only the three owners
One: only the managing member
quiz.explanation: Every individual at 25% or more meets the ownership prong, so all three owners qualify; one control person is added. The 25% owner meets the threshold because it is 25% or more.

quiz.question: A family trust owns 30% of a legal entity customer. Under the beneficial ownership rule, who is the beneficial owner for that stake?
options: Each beneficiary of the trust
The trustee
The person who created the trust
No one, because trusts are excluded
quiz.explanation: Where a trust owns 25% or more, the rule treats the trustee as the beneficial owner under the ownership prong.

quiz.question: The person opening an account certifies the beneficial owners. The next day Elena learns from public records that an undisclosed company owns 60% of the customer. What should she do?
options: Rely on the signed certification, because the bank may always rely on whatever the person opening the account certifies in good faith, whatever it later learns
Open the account and note the issue for the annual review
Close the file without telling anyone
Stop relying on the certification, obtain correct information and verify the individuals behind the 60% owner, escalating if needed
quiz.explanation: Reliance on the customer's information holds only if the bank has no knowledge of facts that reasonably call it into question. Here it does, so the bank must resolve the discrepancy.

quiz.question: Under FinCEN's February 2026 exceptive relief, what generally changed for existing legal entity customers?
options: Banks generally need not re-identify and re-verify beneficial owners each time the customer opens a new account, unless risk calls for it
Banks no longer need to identify beneficial owners at all
Banks must now re-verify owners every year
Banks may now rely entirely on FinCEN's beneficial ownership registry instead of collecting and verifying owner information from customers themselves
quiz.explanation: The relief removed routine repeat identification and verification at each new account opening for existing legal entity customers, subject to risk-based exceptions. The underlying duty remains.

quiz.question: A US-formed company tells Bramblecove it no longer has to report beneficial ownership to FinCEN, so the bank shouldn't ask. What is accurate?
options: The customer is right; banks now rely on FinCEN's registry
The bank may skip the ownership prong for exempt US companies but must still identify and verify one control person for the account
Its BOI filing exemption under the Corporate Transparency Act rules does not remove the bank's own beneficial ownership duty
The exemption applies to banks as well as companies
quiz.explanation: FinCEN's 2026 final rule limits BOI reporting to foreign reporting companies, but banks still must identify and verify beneficial owners under 31 CFR 1010.230.

quiz.question: For how long must Bramblecove keep the identifying information it obtained under its CIP?
options: Five years after the account is opened
Three years after the last transaction
Ten years after the record is made
Five years after the account is closed
quiz.explanation: Identifying information is kept for five years after the account is closed. Descriptions of documents, methods and discrepancy resolution are kept five years after the record is made.

quiz.question: Which statement about ongoing customer due diligence under the bank program rule is correct?
options: It means re-running the full Customer Identification Program on every customer every year and recording the results again in each customer's file
It includes understanding the nature and purpose of relationships to build a risk profile and monitoring to report suspicious transactions
It applies only to legal entity customers
It is optional guidance in the FFIEC manual
quiz.explanation: The program rule requires risk-based ongoing CDD: a customer risk profile based on the nature and purpose of the relationship, ongoing monitoring, and risk-based updating of customer information including beneficial owners.

sessions.title: Enhanced Due Diligence: Correspondent and Private Banking
sessions.summary: Due diligence for foreign correspondent accounts, enhanced due diligence for higher-risk foreign banks, the shell bank ban and private banking for senior foreign political figures.
objectives: Apply the risk factors and periodic review for foreign correspondent accounts
Identify which foreign banks require enhanced due diligence and what it involves
Apply the shell bank prohibition and certification safe harbor
Apply private banking due diligence and enhanced scrutiny for senior foreign political figures

cards.title: Kevin's two big wins
cards.setting: Correspondent and private banking desk, Bramblecove Bank, Miami. 9:00 am.

lines.text: Big week. Banco Isla Verde wants a US dollar correspondent account with us, and a new private banking client is moving USD 6m across.
Isla Verde holds an offshore banking license. That alone changes the due diligence we owe.
And the private client is a holding company. The real owner is Mr. Arturo Calden, a serving foreign finance minister.
So we have a foreign correspondent account that needs enhanced due diligence, and a private banking account with a senior foreign political figure behind it.
And we need to be sure Isla Verde isn't a shell, or a doorway for other banks we've never met.
Stage three: the Correspondent Desk. These are some of the highest-risk accounts a US bank keeps.

cards.title: Due diligence for foreign correspondent accounts

scenes.heading: Every foreign correspondent account
scenes.narration: Under 31 CFR 1010.610, a US bank needs a risk-based due diligence program for every correspondent account it keeps for a foreign financial institution, as part of its AML program.

scenes.heading: Assess the risk
scenes.narration: The bank weighs the foreign institution's business and markets, the account's type, purpose and expected activity, the length of the relationship, the home country's AML and supervisory regime, and the institution's AML record.

scenes.heading: Review the activity
scenes.narration: Controls include a periodic review of account activity to check it still matches the stated type, purpose and anticipated activity.

scenes.heading: Enhanced due diligence
scenes.narration: Foreign banks with an offshore banking license, or licensed in a country designated as non-cooperative or as warranting special measures, get enhanced due diligence: their AML program, transaction monitoring, nested banks and, if not publicly traded, their owners.

scenes.heading: When you cannot do it
scenes.narration: If due diligence cannot be performed, the bank's procedures must say when to refuse to open the account, suspend activity, file a SAR or close the account.

cards.title: From all correspondents to enhanced scrutiny

items.label: All foreign correspondent accounts
items.detail: Risk-based due diligence program for every account kept for a foreign financial institution

items.label: Risk assessment of each account
items.detail: Business, account purpose, relationship, home regime, AML record

items.label: Foreign banks in the EDD categories
items.detail: Offshore license, non-cooperative country designation, or special measures designation

items.label: Enhanced due diligence
items.detail: AML program review, monitoring, nested bank checks, owners of non-public banks

cards.question: Banco Isla Verde operates under an offshore banking license. What does that mean for Bramblecove's correspondent account?
options: Nothing extra, if the bank is profitable
The account must receive enhanced due diligence under 31 CFR 1010.610(b)
The account is prohibited outright
Only OFAC screening is required
cards.explanation: A foreign bank operating under an offshore banking license is one of the categories that require enhanced due diligence. It is not banned outright; the shell bank prohibition is a different test.

cards.title: Risk factors and the questions behind them
cards.prompt: Match each risk factor in 1010.610 to the question Kevin's team should ask.

pairs.left: Nature of the business and markets
pairs.right: Who are Isla Verde's customers and where do they operate?
What payments will flow, in what volumes and for what reason?

pairs.left: Nature and duration of the relationship
pairs.right: Have we or our affiliates dealt with this bank before, and for how long?
How strong are AML laws and supervision where Isla Verde is licensed and where its owners are incorporated?
What is known or reasonably available about its past AML failures or enforcement?

cards.title: The shell bank ban (31 CFR 1010.630)
cards.body:
A US bank **must not** establish, maintain, administer or manage a correspondent account in the United States **for a foreign shell bank**. It must also take **reasonable steps** so that a foreign bank's correspondent account is **not used indirectly** to provide banking services to a shell bank. The rule does not stop services to a shell's **regulated affiliate**.

For each foreign bank correspondent, the US bank keeps records in the United States of the **owners** (if its shares are not publicly traded) and of a **US-resident agent** authorised to accept legal process.

**Safe harbor:** the bank is treated as compliant if it obtains a **certification or recertification** from the foreign bank **at least once every three years**. If it later knows or suspects that certified information is wrong, it must ask the foreign bank to verify or correct it, or take other steps.

cards.title: Prohibited, enhanced or general?
cards.prompt: Sort each foreign correspondent request by the level of response the rules call for.

items.text: A bank with no physical presence anywhere and no regulated affiliate
A respondent that would let a shell bank use our account through its own account
A bank operating under an offshore banking license
A bank licensed in a country Treasury designated as warranting special measures
A bank licensed in a country designated non-cooperative by a body the US belongs to, with US concurrence
A large, publicly traded bank in a well-supervised country, outside the EDD categories
A regional bank in a well-supervised country seeking a trade-payments account

cards.title: The minister's holding company
cards.setting: Private banking suite, Miami. Mr. Calden's lawyer is on speakerphone.

lines.text: The lawyer says the USD 6m comes from 'family investments' and the account will be used for property purchases in Florida.
Mr. Calden is a serving finance minister. For a private banking account, the rule asks us to find out if an owner is a senior foreign political figure, and he is.
So we refuse? He's a great client.
Not automatically. We apply enhanced scrutiny designed to detect proceeds of foreign corruption. If we can't do proper due diligence, our procedures tell us what's next.

cards.title: Private banking accounts (31 CFR 1010.620)
cards.body:
For private banking accounts, the bank's due diligence program must take reasonable steps to:

- identify **all nominal and beneficial owners**
- find out whether any of them is a **senior foreign political figure**
- establish the **source of funds** and the **purpose and expected use** of the account
- **review activity** against that information and report suspicious activity

Where a senior foreign political figure is a nominal or beneficial owner, the bank applies **enhanced scrutiny** designed to detect and report the **proceeds of foreign corruption**: assets gained through misappropriation of public funds, unlawful conversion of state property, bribery or extortion.

If due diligence cannot be performed, procedures must say when to refuse, suspend, file a SAR or close.

For other politically exposed customers, a **2020 joint statement** by the agencies and FinCEN explains that PEP status alone does not trigger extra requirements: due diligence follows the customer's actual risk.

cards.title: Mr. Calden's account
cards.situation: The holding company's beneficial owner is a serving foreign finance minister. The lawyer describes the USD 6m as 'family investments' but will not provide documents, saying the minister's privacy must be protected. Kevin is under pressure to open the account before quarter end.

choices.text: Open the account; the minister is a public figure, so the risk is known
choices.outcome: Being well known is not due diligence. The rule requires the source of funds and enhanced scrutiny for proceeds of foreign corruption; neither has been done.

choices.text: Ask for documented evidence of the source of funds and wealth, apply enhanced scrutiny, and if the client will not provide it, follow procedures to refuse and consider a SAR
choices.outcome: Best answer. This applies 1010.620: identify owners, establish source of funds and purpose, apply enhanced scrutiny, and use the procedures for when due diligence cannot be performed.

choices.text: Open the account but limit deposits to USD 1m until documents arrive
choices.outcome: Partly right in spirit, but the account would be operating without the required due diligence and enhanced scrutiny, and the limit has no basis in the facts.

choices.text: Refuse because the bank should never bank foreign politicians
choices.outcome: The rules do not ban these clients. They require risk-based enhanced scrutiny, and blanket refusals are not what the agencies expect.

cards.title: Correspondent versus private banking due diligence

items.label: Who
items.left: Accounts kept for foreign financial institutions
items.right: Private banking accounts kept in the US

items.label: Core steps
items.left: Risk assessment on five factors plus periodic activity review
items.right: Owners, political figure check, source of funds, purpose, activity review

items.label: Enhanced trigger
items.left: Offshore license, non-cooperative or special measures country
items.right: A senior foreign political figure as nominal or beneficial owner

items.label: Enhanced focus
items.left: AML program, monitoring, nested banks, owners at 10% or more
items.right: Detecting proceeds of foreign corruption

items.label: If you can't
items.left: Refuse, suspend, file a SAR or close
items.right: Refuse, suspend, file a SAR or close

cards.title: Real case: Bank of America, 2026
cards.body:
On **13 October 2026 FinCEN** assessed a **USD 1.2 billion** civil money penalty against **Bank of America, N.A.** for failing to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese money laundering networks and illicit finance along the southwest border. The **OCC** assessed a **USD 750 million** penalty the same day for a deficient BSA/AML program, and **OFAC** announced a separate sanctions settlement.

In its resolution with FinCEN, the bank admitted it **willfully** violated the BSA by failing to:

- implement and maintain an AML program meeting the minimum requirements
- conduct **due diligence for correspondent accounts** of foreign financial institutions
- file **Suspicious Activity Reports**

**Lesson:** correspondent due diligence is not paperwork at onboarding; it is a live control examined alongside monitoring and SAR filing.

Source: FinCEN press release and consent order 2026-03 (fincen.gov).

cards.front: Payable-through account
cards.back: A correspondent account through which a foreign bank lets its own customers carry out US banking activity directly or through subaccounts. EDD includes learning who can direct transactions through it.

cards.front: Nested correspondent use
cards.back: When the foreign bank lets other foreign banks use its account with you. EDD asks you to find out and assess those banks.

cards.front: Owner (for EDD on a non-public foreign bank)
cards.back: Anyone who directly or indirectly owns, controls or can vote 10% or more of any class of the foreign bank's securities.

cards.front: Foreign shell bank
cards.back: A foreign bank without a physical presence in any country. US banks may not keep correspondent accounts for one, except via a regulated affiliate.

cards.front: Proceeds of foreign corruption
cards.back: Assets a senior foreign political figure gains by misappropriating public funds, converting state property, or through bribery or extortion.

cards.title: Onboarding a foreign correspondent
cards.prompt: Put Kevin's onboarding steps for Banco Isla Verde in order.
steps: Determine whether Isla Verde falls into an enhanced due diligence category
Assess the account's money laundering risk across the required factors
Obtain the shell bank certification and record owners and the US agent for legal process
Review Isla Verde's AML program and ask whether it lets other foreign banks use the account
Approve with monitoring set to the expected activity, or refuse if diligence cannot be done
Review activity periodically against the stated purpose and recertify within three years

cards.question: Bramblecove holds a shell bank certification from a foreign bank obtained two years ago. Marcus now has reason to suspect a key fact in it is wrong. What should the bank do?
options: Nothing until the three-year recertification is due
Ask the foreign bank to verify or correct the information, or take other steps to establish the facts
Close the account immediately without contacting the bank
Ask the respondent's customers directly
cards.explanation: The certification safe harbor depends on interim verification: when the bank knows or suspects information is no longer correct, it must ask the foreign bank to verify or correct it, or take other appropriate measures. Waiting for the three-year cycle loses the safe harbor.

cards.title: Correspondent Desk secured
items: Every foreign correspondent account needs risk-based due diligence and periodic activity review.
Offshore licenses and non-cooperative or special measures countries trigger enhanced due diligence.
No correspondent accounts for foreign shell banks, directly or indirectly; certify at least every three years.
Private banking: owners, political figures, source of funds, purpose; enhanced scrutiny for senior foreign political figures.
If due diligence cannot be done, follow procedures to refuse, suspend, file a SAR or close.

cards.prompt: If you work near correspondent or private banking, where does commercial pressure most often meet due diligence in your team? How would you raise a concern before an account is opened rather than after?

quiz.question: Which foreign bank requires enhanced due diligence on its correspondent account under 31 CFR 1010.610(c)?
options: One operating under an offshore banking license
Any foreign bank with more than ten branches
Any foreign bank that is publicly traded
Any foreign bank opening a US dollar account
quiz.explanation: The EDD categories are banks with an offshore banking license, banks licensed in countries designated non-cooperative by a body the US belongs to (with US concurrence), and banks licensed in countries designated for special measures.

quiz.question: For a foreign bank in an EDD category whose shares are not publicly traded, whose identity must Bramblecove determine?
options: Every shareholder of the foreign bank, however small the holding, together with each director and senior officer
Only the chief executive
Each owner who owns, controls or can vote 10% or more of any class of its securities
Only owners above 50%
quiz.explanation: EDD includes identifying each owner of a non-publicly traded foreign bank and the extent of their interest; 'owner' means 10% or more of any class of securities, with family members treated as one person.

quiz.question: A foreign respondent bank lets five smaller foreign banks send payments through its account at Bramblecove. Under EDD, what must Bramblecove do?
options: Nothing further, because the due diligence duty covers only the direct respondent bank and not any banks that use its account
Close the account immediately
Report each smaller bank to OFAC
Find out about those banks' use of the account and take reasonable steps to assess and mitigate the risk
quiz.explanation: EDD requires the bank to determine whether the foreign bank provides correspondent accounts to other foreign banks that use the US account and, if so, to obtain information to assess and mitigate those risks.

quiz.question: What does the shell bank rule prohibit?
options: Any account for a foreign bank's regulated affiliate
Keeping a US correspondent account for a foreign bank that has no physical presence in any country
All correspondent accounts for offshore-licensed banks
Any account for a company with no employees
quiz.explanation: A US bank may not keep a correspondent account for a foreign shell bank, and must take reasonable steps to stop indirect use. Services to a shell's regulated affiliate are not prohibited.

quiz.question: How often must Bramblecove obtain a certification or recertification from a foreign respondent bank to stay within the shell bank safe harbor?
options: Every year
Every five years
At least once every three years
Only at account opening
quiz.explanation: The safe harbor applies when the bank obtains a certification or recertification at least once every three years, plus interim verification when it suspects information is wrong.

quiz.question: A private banking client's beneficial owner is a serving foreign minister. What does 31 CFR 1010.620 require in addition to standard private banking due diligence?
options: Enhanced scrutiny reasonably designed to detect and report transactions that may involve proceeds of foreign corruption
Automatic refusal of the account
Approval from the State Department
Monthly reporting of the account's activity to FinCEN, together with a copy of the client's source of wealth evidence and tax returns
quiz.explanation: Where a senior foreign political figure is a nominal or beneficial owner, the program must include enhanced scrutiny designed to detect and report proceeds of foreign corruption. The rule does not ban such accounts.

quiz.question: Mr. Calden's lawyer refuses to document the source of USD 6m for a private banking account, citing privacy. Kevin wants to open the account anyway. What should the bank's procedures lead to?
options: Open it, since the client is a public figure
Treat it as due diligence that cannot be performed: consider refusing the account and whether to file a SAR
Open it with a lower deposit limit and no further steps, then complete the source-of-funds review after the quarter-end deadline
Ask OFAC for permission to open it
quiz.explanation: 1010.620 requires the source of funds and enhanced scrutiny; where due diligence cannot be performed, procedures must say when to refuse, suspend, file a SAR or close.

quiz.question: A relationship manager says, 'Every PEP must automatically get enhanced due diligence under US rules.' What is the most accurate response?
options: Correct; every politically exposed person, foreign or domestic, must receive the same enhanced due diligence in all account types
Wrong; US rules never mention political figures
Correct, but only for customers above USD 1m
Enhanced scrutiny is required for senior foreign political figures in private banking; otherwise diligence follows risk
quiz.explanation: The explicit duty is in 1010.620 for private banking accounts with a senior foreign political figure. The 2020 joint statement says PEP status alone does not create extra requirements; due diligence is risk-based.

quiz.question: Which factor must Bramblecove consider when assessing the money laundering risk of a foreign correspondent account?
options: The AML and supervisory regime of the country that licensed the foreign bank
The foreign bank's credit rating only
Whether the foreign bank uses US software
The nationality of the relationship manager
quiz.explanation: The rule's factors include the foreign institution's business and markets, the account's type and purpose, the relationship, the licensing country's AML and supervisory regime, and the institution's AML record.

quiz.question: In the 2026 FinCEN action against Bank of America, which failure linked to this stage did the bank admit?
options: Opening accounts for foreign shell banks
Failing to file CTRs on teller cash
Failing to conduct due diligence for correspondent accounts of foreign financial institutions
Breaching the Corporate Transparency Act by failing to report its own beneficial owners to FinCEN's registry
quiz.explanation: Bank of America admitted it willfully failed to maintain a compliant AML program, conduct due diligence for foreign correspondent accounts and file SARs. FinCEN's penalty was USD 1.2 billion.

sessions.title: SARs, CTRs, Records and Confidentiality
sessions.summary: When and how to file suspicious activity reports and currency transaction reports, how to keep BSA records, and how to protect SAR confidentiality.
objectives: Apply the SAR threshold, suspicion categories and filing deadlines
Apply CTR thresholds, aggregation and filing rules, and recognise structuring
Protect SAR confidentiality, including when subpoenaed or asked by a customer
Know the main BSA record and retention rules

cards.title: Nine deposits under ten thousand
cards.setting: Investigations room, Columbus, with the Houston and Miami branches on screen. 2:15 pm.

lines.text: Alert on Coastal Tile Supply. Nine cash deposits in four days, each between USD 9,000 and USD 9,800, spread over three branches.
My teller says the depositor asked her, 'Does the bank report anything under ten?' Then he took back two bills.
That question matters. Amounts near the threshold alone don't require a SAR. Information that someone is trying to avoid the report does.
Also, a lawyer emailed asking for 'any suspicious activity reports filed on my client.' Different client, same week.
Stage four is the Reporting Room: SARs, CTRs, records and the secrecy that protects them.

cards.title: The SAR rule for banks (31 CFR 1020.320)

scenes.heading: When a SAR is required
scenes.narration: A bank must report a transaction conducted or attempted by, at or through it that involves or adds up to at least 5,000 dollars, if it knows, suspects or has reason to suspect it is suspicious.

scenes.heading: Three kinds of suspicion
scenes.narration: Funds from illegal activity or hiding them; a transaction designed to evade BSA requirements, such as structuring; or a transaction with no business or apparent lawful purpose that is unusual for the customer, with no reasonable explanation after review.

scenes.heading: Thirty days
scenes.narration: File no later than 30 calendar days after first detecting facts that may justify a SAR. If no suspect is identified, the bank may take another 30 days, but never more than 60 days in total.

scenes.heading: Urgent cases
scenes.narration: For violations that need immediate attention, such as ongoing money laundering schemes, the bank also notifies law enforcement by telephone straight away, and still files the SAR on time.

scenes.heading: Keep it secret, keep it safe
scenes.narration: A SAR and anything that would reveal it are confidential. The bank keeps a copy and the supporting documents for five years from filing, and is protected from liability for the report.

cards.title: The SAR clock
cards.caption: Continuing-activity timing is optional guidance: the October 2025 FAQs confirm banks are not required to run separate continuing activity reviews.

items.label: Initial detection
items.detail: Facts that may be a basis for filing are first detected

items.label: SAR due
items.detail: Deadline when a suspect is identified

items.label: Latest possible filing
items.detail: Only if no suspect was identified at detection

items.label: End of 90-day period
items.detail: Under optional continuing-activity guidance, after a Day 30 filing

items.label: Continuing activity SAR
items.detail: Optional timing if the bank follows that guidance

cards.question: Marcus first detects facts that may justify a SAR on 1 March and has identified the suspect. By when must Bramblecove file?
options: Within 15 days
No later than 30 calendar days after 1 March
Within 60 days, because complex cases get extra time
By the end of the quarter
cards.explanation: With a suspect identified, the deadline is 30 calendar days after initial detection. The extra 30 days (60 in total) is only available when no suspect was identified on the date of detection. Fifteen days is the CTR filing period.

cards.title: Currency transaction reports and structuring
cards.body:
Banks file a **CTR** for each deposit, withdrawal, exchange or other payment or transfer involving **currency of more than USD 10,000** (31 CFR 1010.311).

- **Aggregation:** multiple cash transactions count as one if the bank knows they are by or for the same person and total **more than USD 10,000 cash-in or cash-out in one business day**. All domestic branches count as one bank. Night, weekend and holiday deposits count on the next business day.
- **Deadline:** file within **15 days** after the transaction and keep a copy for **five years**.
- **Exemptions:** the rules let banks exempt certain customers from CTRs under conditions in 31 CFR 1020.315; follow your bank's procedures.

**Structuring**, breaking up cash in any manner to evade a CTR, is unlawful. The **October 2025 FAQs** confirm that activity near the threshold is not on its own enough to require a SAR; a SAR is required when the bank knows, suspects or has reason to suspect the transactions are **designed to evade** reporting.

cards.title: SAR, CTR or neither?
cards.prompt: Based only on these facts, sort each event by the report Bramblecove must file.

items.text: A customer deposits USD 12,500 in cash in one visit, for a normal business reason
The same person deposits USD 6,000 cash in Houston and USD 5,000 in Chicago on one business day, and the bank knows it
A depositor asks how to avoid a report, then splits USD 18,000 into amounts below USD 10,000 over several days
A USD 40,000 wire unusual for the customer, with no business or apparent lawful purpose found after review
A restaurant deposits USD 9,700 cash, in line with years of similar deposits, with no sign of evasion
A branch robbery that has been reported to law enforcement

cards.title: The lawyer's request
cards.setting: Legal and BSA conference room, Columbus. The next morning.

lines.text: The lawyer has now sent a subpoena in a private lawsuit asking for 'all SARs and SAR drafts' about his client.
Meanwhile the Coastal Tile owner phoned the branch: 'Did you report me to the government?'
Two tests of the same principle. Nobody at this bank discloses a SAR or anything that reveals one exists, to the customer or to a private litigant.
Let's work out exactly how each person should respond.

cards.title: Subpoenaed for a SAR
cards.situation: A private litigant's subpoena asks Bramblecove for all SARs about a customer. The bank did file a SAR. A junior paralegal suggests sending the SAR 'because subpoenas must be obeyed', while another colleague suggests replying 'no SAR exists' to end the matter.

choices.text: Produce the SAR, because a subpoena overrides bank policy
choices.outcome: Wrong. The SAR rule requires the bank to decline to produce a SAR or information revealing one, even when subpoenaed.

choices.text: Reply that no SAR exists
choices.outcome: Wrong. A false denial is not the answer; the bank declines without confirming or denying, and must not mislead.

choices.text: Decline to produce any SAR or information revealing one, cite the SAR confidentiality rule, notify FinCEN of the request and the response, and involve legal counsel
choices.outcome: Best answer. This follows 31 CFR 1020.320(e): decline, cite the rule and the statute, and notify FinCEN.

choices.text: Decline the request but do not tell FinCEN, since nothing was disclosed
choices.outcome: Partly right: declining is correct, but the rule also requires the bank to notify FinCEN of the request and its response.

cards.front: May Bramblecove share a SAR with its examining regulator?
cards.back: Yes. Disclosure to FinCEN, law enforcement or the federal or state regulator examining BSA compliance is permitted, as long as no person involved is notified.

cards.front: May Bramblecove share the underlying facts with another bank?
cards.back: Yes, the underlying facts and documents may be shared to prepare a joint SAR, without revealing a SAR to anyone involved in the activity.

cards.front: Must the bank document every decision not to file a SAR?
cards.back: No. The 2025 FAQs say there is no requirement to document it, though a short note is often sensible under the bank's procedures.

cards.front: Must the bank run a separate review after each SAR to see if activity continued?
cards.back: No. The 2025 FAQs say risk-based monitoring may be relied on instead; the 90-day continuing activity approach is optional.

cards.front: Is the bank liable to the customer for filing a SAR?
cards.back: The rule gives a safe harbor from liability to any person for the disclosure, to the extent the statute provides.

cards.title: When a customer asks 'Did you report me?'
cards.body:
- Do **not** confirm, deny or hint. 'We follow federal rules for all customers' is enough.
- Do **not** say 'compliance is looking at your account' or change your manner in a way that signals a report.
- Answer factual CTR questions with the standard script if your bank has one; never coach a customer on avoiding a report.
- Log the conversation and tell the investigator. A question about reporting can itself be a red flag.

items.label: SAR threshold for banks
items.detail: Involves or aggregates at least this amount, plus suspicion

items.label: SAR deadline
items.detail: After initial detection; up to 60 if no suspect identified

items.label: CTR trigger
items.detail: Currency in or out, aggregated per person per business day

items.label: CTR filing
items.detail: After the day of the reportable transaction

items.label: Funds transfer records
items.detail: Originator, amount, date, instructions, beneficiary's bank

items.label: BSA record retention
items.detail: General period for records, SARs with supporting documents and CTR copies

cards.title: What record, kept how?
cards.prompt: Match each BSA record to its rule.

pairs.right: Kept five years from filing; supporting documents are treated as filed with the SAR
Kept five years from the date of the report

pairs.left: Funds transfer of USD 3,000 or more
pairs.right: Originator's bank keeps originator name and address, amount, date, instructions and beneficiary's bank
Kept five years after the account is closed

pairs.left: Records required by 31 CFR Chapter X generally
pairs.right: Kept five years and accessible within a reasonable time

cards.title: Real case: USAA Federal Savings Bank, 2022
cards.body:
In **March 2022 FinCEN** imposed a **USD 140 million** civil money penalty on **USAA Federal Savings Bank**, crediting a **USD 60 million** OCC penalty for the same conduct. The bank admitted willful violations.

FinCEN found that the bank:

- **willfully failed to timely and accurately file at least 3,873 SARs**
- let backlogs build to around **90,000 un-reviewed alerts** and **6,900 un-reviewed cases** by the end of 2021, because it had not hired enough staff
- moved to a new monitoring system that failed to flag cases the old system caught, cases that had led to SARs

**Lessons:** the 30-day SAR clock only works if alerts are reviewed; system changes need testing against the old results; and staffing is part of the program, not an afterthought.

Source: FinCEN enforcement action 2022-01 (fincen.gov).

cards.question: Elena's teller is asked by Coastal Tile's owner whether the bank 'filed something with the government' about him. A SAR has been filed. What is the right response?
options: Confirm it, because the customer has a right to know
Deny it, to keep the customer calm
Neither confirm nor deny, give a neutral answer and report the conversation to BSA/AML
Tell him a CTR was filed instead
cards.explanation: No bank employee may disclose a SAR or information that would reveal one. A false denial or a misleading statement is not the answer either. A neutral reply and escalation protects the report and the investigation.

cards.title: Reporting Room decoded
items: SAR: USD 5,000 or more plus knowledge or suspicion; file within 30 days of detection, 60 at most if no suspect.
SARs and anything revealing them are confidential; decline subpoenas, cite the rule and notify FinCEN.
CTR: cash of more than USD 10,000, aggregated per person per business day; file within 15 days.
Near-threshold cash alone is not a SAR; information showing intent to evade reporting is.
Most BSA records, SAR files and CTR copies are kept five years; funds transfers of USD 3,000+ need originator records.

cards.prompt: Think of a question a customer might ask you about cash or reporting. How would you answer it in your own words without coaching them or revealing anything, and whom would you tell afterwards?

quiz.question: What is the dollar amount at which a bank's suspicious activity reporting duty begins under 31 CFR 1020.320, where the bank knows or suspects the transaction is suspicious?
options: Transactions over USD 10,000
Transactions of USD 3,000 or more
Transactions involving or aggregating at least USD 5,000
Any amount, without exception
quiz.explanation: Banks must report transactions that involve or aggregate at least USD 5,000 where the bank knows, suspects or has reason to suspect they fall in a suspicious category. Banks may also file voluntarily below that.

quiz.question: Bramblecove detects suspicious facts but has not identified any suspect. What is the latest it may file the SAR?
options: 30 calendar days after initial detection
60 calendar days after initial detection
90 calendar days after initial detection
15 days after the transaction
quiz.explanation: If no suspect is identified at detection, the bank may take an extra 30 days to identify one, but reporting may not be delayed more than 60 calendar days after initial detection.

quiz.question: A customer deposits USD 9,000 in cash at the Houston branch in the morning and USD 2,000 at the Chicago branch that afternoon. Bramblecove's systems link both to her. What must the bank file?
options: A CTR, because the cash deposits by the same person exceed USD 10,000 in one business day
Nothing, because each deposit is under USD 10,000
A SAR only, because deposits made at different branches on the same day are never added together for currency reporting
A CTR only if she asks for one
quiz.explanation: Multiple cash transactions known to be by or for the same person are aggregated across all domestic branches; together they exceed USD 10,000 in one business day, so a CTR is required.

quiz.question: A grocery store deposits USD 9,600 in cash twice a week, matching years of history. There is no sign of evasion. According to the October 2025 FAQs, is a SAR required?
options: Yes; any deposit near USD 10,000 is structuring
Yes, but only after three months
No, because grocery stores are exempt from SARs
No; amounts at or near the CTR threshold alone are not enough to require a SAR
quiz.explanation: The FAQs confirm that the mere presence of transactions near the threshold does not require a SAR. A SAR is required if the bank knows, suspects or has reason to suspect the transactions are designed to evade reporting.

quiz.question: A depositor asks a teller, 'How much can I bring in without the bank reporting it?' and then splits cash across days. Which report should the teller's escalation lead to?
options: No report at all, because each separate deposit stayed below the currency transaction reporting threshold
A CTR only for the largest deposit
An OFAC report through the OFAC Reporting System
A SAR, because information suggests the transactions are designed to evade CTR reporting
quiz.explanation: Structuring to evade a CTR is unlawful, and a SAR is required when the bank knows, suspects or has reason to suspect transactions are designed to evade reporting. The customer's question is key information.

quiz.question: Bramblecove receives a subpoena from a private litigant requesting any SARs on a customer. What does the SAR rule require?
options: Produce the SAR under seal
Decline to produce the SAR or information revealing it, cite the rule and statute, and notify FinCEN
Produce the SAR if the judge signed the subpoena
Confirm to the court that a SAR exists but withhold its content, since only the narrative itself is protected
quiz.explanation: Under 31 CFR 1020.320(e), a bank subpoenaed for a SAR or information revealing one must decline, cite the rule and statute, and notify FinCEN of the request and its response.

quiz.question: Which disclosure of SAR-related information is permitted, provided nobody involved in the activity is notified?
